en: *Laghusiddhāntakaumudī*: Now begins the section on technical terms (*saṃjñā*). "The final consonant [in a *pratyāhāra*] is [the name of the preceding vowel]. (Pāṇini 1.3.3)
In an original instruction (upadeśa), the final consonant (hal) is to be understood as having the marker *it*. An "original instruction" refers to the first pronunciation [of a word].
In all cases, a word not seen within a particular rule (*sūtra*) is to be supplied from another rule.
Non-appearance is elision.
The non-appearance of that which has become applicable shall be designated as *lopa* (elision).
There is elision of that [element].

There shall be elision (lopa) of that [final phoneme] here. The letters beginning with Ṇa (ṇādi) serve the purpose of those beginning with AṆ (aṇādi). "The first [phoneme], together with the final indicatory letter (it), [denotes the entire class]. (Pāṇini 1.1.71)

The first [letter] together with the final [indicatory letter] shall be the designation (saṃjñā) for itself and for those situated between it; for example, "aṇ" is the designation for the phonemes a, i, and u.
In the same way, there are such designations as "ac," "hal," and "al."
A vowel has the designation *hrasva* (short), *dīrgha* (long), or *pluta* (protracted) according to its duration of one, two, or three *mātrās*.
*u*, *ū*, and *ū3* are *vaḥ*;
that vowel (*ac*) whose duration is one, two, or three *mātrās* respectively shall be designated as short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), and protracted (*pluta*).
Each of these is further divided into three types according to the distinctions of acute (*udātta*) and so forth.
A vowel pronounced with high pitch is called udātta (acute).
A low-pitched vowel is called *anudātta*.
The combination [of vowels] is called *svarati*.
That [consonant], though ninefold, is further divided into two types each—nasalized and non-nasalized.
A sound articulated through both the mouth and the nose is called *anunāsika* (nasalized).
A phoneme pronounced through the mouth, the teeth, and the nose shall be designated as *anunāsika* (nasalized).
Thus, for these phonemes—a, i, u, and ṛ—there are eighteen varieties each;
for the phoneme ḷ, there are twelve.
Because it lacks long vowels;
likewise, there are twelve for the *ec* vowels as well, because they lack short vowels.
Those sounds produced with the same place and effort of articulation are homogeneous (savarṇa).

That pair consisting of the place of articulation—such as the palate—and the internal effort, which is common to two [sounds], shall be designated as *savarṇa* (homogeneous) with respect to one another.
(It should be stated that there is mutual *savarṇa*-status between the sounds *ṛ* and *ḷ*). The throat is the place of articulation for the sounds *a*, *ku* (the velars), and *visarjanīya*.
The palate is the place of articulation for *icuyaśāḥ*; the roof of the mouth for *ṛṭuraṣāḥ*;
and the teeth for *ḷtulasāḥ*.
The lips are the place of articulation for the *upadhmānīya* and *upū*.
For *ña*, *ma*, *ṅa*, *ṇa*, and *na*, it is the nose as well. For *e* and *ai*, it is the throat and the palate.
The *odaūt* sounds are articulated at the throat and lips;
the *va* sound is articulated at the teeth and lips;
and the *jihvāmūlīya* is articulated at the root of the tongue.

Regarding the nasal sound (*anusvāra*) produced through the nose, effort is twofold: internal and external. The former is fivefold, based on the distinctions of contact (*spṛṣṭa*), slight contact (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*), slightly open (*īṣadvivṛta*), open (*vivṛta*), and closed (*saṃvṛta*).
Among those, the articulation of the *sparśa* consonants is "touched" (*spṛṣṭa*);
that of the semivowels (*antaḥstha*) is "slightly touched" (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*);
and that of the sibilants (*ūṣman*) is "slightly opened" (*īṣadvivṛta*).
The vowels are *vivṛta* (open).
In actual usage, the short *a*-sound is *saṃvṛta* (closed); however, during the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*), it remains *vivṛta*.

The external effort (bāhyaprayatna), however, is of eleven kinds: opening (vivāra), closure (saṃvāra), breath (śvāsa), resonance (nāda), voiced (ghoṣa), unvoiced (aghoṣa), weak aspiration (alpaprāṇa), strong aspiration (mahāprāṇa), acute (udātta), grave (anudātta), and circumflex (svarita). The *khara* consonants are characterized by opening, breath, and being unvoiced; the *haś* consonants are characterized by closure, resonance, and being voiced.

The first, third, and fifth letters of the classes (varga), as well as the semi-vowels (yaṇ), are of weak breath (alpaprāṇa). The second and fourth letters of the classes, as well as the sibilants and h (śala), are of strong breath (mahāprāṇa).
The consonants from k to m are the stops (sparśa).
The *yaṇ* sounds are the semivowels (*antaḥstha*).
The *śal* sounds are the sibilants and aspirates (*ūṣman*). The *ac* sounds are the vowels (*svara*).
The *jihvāmūlīya* occurs after *ka* and *kha*, resembling a half-*visarga*;
the *upadhmānīya* occurs after *pa* and *pha*, resembling a half-*visarga*.
The *anusvāra* and *visarga* occur respectively after the vowels *aṃ* and *aḥ*.
An *it* (a vowel with an indicatory letter) and that which is not a suffix (*apratyaya*) are also [designated by their own name] when they are homogeneous (*savarṇa*) with another sound.
That which is understood as being prescribed is a *pratyaya*.

A vowel (*aṇ*) that is not being prescribed, as well as one followed by an *it*, shall be the designation for its homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*). In this very context, *aṇ* [is defined] by means of a subsequent *ṇakāra*.
*ku*, *cu*, *ṭu*, *tu*, and *pu* are thus declared.
Therefore, in this way, *a* is the designation for eighteen [sounds];
likewise are *i* and *u*.
The vowel *ṛ* [is the substitute] for thirty; likewise, the vowel *ḷ* is also [the substitute] for thirty;
and the diphthongs (*ec*) are [the substitutes] for twelve.
The *ya*, *va*, *la*, and *ra* sounds are each twofold, distinguished by being nasal (*anunāsika*) or non-nasal (*ananunāsika*).
Therefore, those non-nasal ones are the designations for each pair [of homogeneous sounds].
"Closest proximity" (*paraḥ saṃnikarṣaḥ*) refers to consonants joined together (*saṃhatāḥ*).
An excessive proximity of colors would result in a confused mass lacking distinct names.
Conjunction is the contact between contiguous [entities].
Consonants not separated by vowels shall be designated as "conjunctions" (saṃyoga).
A word (pada) consists of that which ends in a nominal suffix (suP) or a verbal suffix (tiṄ).
That which ends in a nominal suffix (subanta) and that which ends in a verbal suffix (tiṅanta) shall be designated as a "word" (pada).
Thus ends the section on technical terms (saṃjñā-prakaraṇa).
Now begins vowel-sandhi (ac-sandhi):
*iko yaṇ aci* (Pāṇini 6.1.77).
In the context of *saṃhitā*, when a vowel follows, one [of the two identical vowels] shall be replaced by a *yaṇ* substitute in its place.
Thus, when *sudhī upāsya* is situated [as the state of the sentence], [the rule applies].
When "in that" (tasmin) is specified, it refers to what precedes.
An operation prescribed by a statement in the locative case (saptamī) should be understood as applying to that which precedes [the cause] and is not separated from it by another phoneme.
In place [of the original], that which is most similar [is substituted].
When such a contingency arises, the most similar substitute should be applied;
thus, when *sudhi* becomes *upāsya*.
And [the doubling does not occur] before a vowel that lacks an *anunāsika*.
According to the rule "A consonant following a vowel may optionally be doubled,
except when it follows a *c*," the letter *dh* is doubled, resulting in *sudhdhy upāsya*.
In the place of *jhal* sounds, *jaś* sounds are substituted before a *jhaś* sound.
This is clear. Thus, the letter *dh* of the preceding [syllable] becomes *d*.
There is the elision of a consonant at the end of a conjunct.
Whatever word ends in a conjunct consonant, there shall be elision of its final [consonant].
The final [element] of that which is designated [by a technical term] is replaced.
When a substitute is prescribed for the final letter of that which is indicated by the genitive case, it would apply to the semivowel *y* here;
however, since the elision (*lopa*) of *y* would otherwise result, it is stated: "The [elision] of *y* is prohibited.
Thus: *suddhyupāsyaḥ*.
Maddhari, Dhātraśa, Lākṛti.
In place of [the sounds] e, o, ay, and āv, [the corresponding guṇa vowels e and o are substituted].
In the sequence of phonemes, *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au* become *ay*, *āv*, *āy*, and *āv* respectively before a vowel.
When there is an enumeration of equal [elements], the assignment [of operations] follows their respective order.
A rule involving an equal number of related elements applies according to their respective order:
*haraye*,
*viṣṇave*.
The Leader; the Purifier.
The [final] *v* or *ān* is elided before the suffix *yi*.
When a suffix beginning with the letter *y* follows, *o* and *au* are replaced by *ava* and *āv*, respectively; as in *gavyam* and *nāvyam*.
(Regarding the atom of distance: a *gavyūti*.
The vowels *a*, *e*, and *o* are termed *guṇa*.
The vowels *e* and *o* shall be designated as *guṇa*.
A suffix denoting the agent of an action occurs after a verbal root when it signifies the time immediately following that of the action expressed by the root.
Since that which follows it is also designated as "para," the term would apply only to that which is articulated at the same time [as the preceding sound].
The substitution of a single guṇa vowel occurs in place of both [sounds] when a vowel follows.
When a vowel follows a non-vowel (avarṇa), a single guṇa substitute shall take the place of both the preceding and the following sounds. For example:
*upendraḥ* and *gaṅgodakam*.
In the context of grammatical instruction, a vowel that does not have an *anunāsika* marker is called *it*.
In this instruction, a nasalized vowel (anunāsika) shall have the designation *ajit*.
The followers of Pāṇini accept the nasalization as an established convention (*pratijñā*).
The letter *r*, when pronounced together with the vowel *a* found in the *laṇ* sūtra, is the technical term for both *r* and *l*.
The *uraṇ* substitutes are followed by *r*.
It has been stated that "ṛ" is the designation for thirty sounds. In its place, the substitute *aṇ* occurs only as being followed by *r*. For example: *kṛṣṇarddhiḥ*.
The syllable *taval*.
There is elision [of *y*] according to Śākalya.
The *y* and *v* at the end of a word, when preceded by a vowel other than *a*, are optionally elided before the suffix *asi*.
That which is not established in what precedes [is considered as not having taken effect].

With respect to the first seven chapters and a quarter (sapādasaptādhyāyī), the final three chapters (tripādī) are not established; likewise, within the tripādī, a subsequent rule is not established with respect to a preceding one.
Thus: *hara iha* becomes *harayiha*.
O Viṣṇu, come here; O Viṣṇu, come here!
The term *vṛddhi* consists of the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au*.
The term 'ādicca' shall have the designation 'vṛddhi'.
Vṛddhi is substituted [for the first vowel] when followed by an *ec* vowel.
When a vowel follows an *āT* vowel, a single substitute *vṛddhi* sound shall take its place. This is an exception to the rule for *guṇa*. Example: *kṛṣṇaikatvam*.
The flood of the Gaṅgā;
the sovereignty of the gods;
the longing for Kṛṣṇa.
The substitution of *e*, *ai*, and *o* for *i*, *ī*, and *u* respectively occurs before the suffixes *eti*, *edhati*, and *ūṭh*.

When a vowel not beginning with *ava* is followed by a vowel beginning with *e* or *ai*, or when *eti* or *edhate* follow, or when the augment *ūṭh* follows, there shall be a single substitute *vṛddhi* [vowel]. Examples:
*upaiti*, *upaidhate*.
*praṣṭhauhaḥ*. Why [is it specified] "of *ejādi*" and so forth? [Consider: *upetaḥ*;
*mā bhavān predidhat*.
(There is the inclusion of *ūha* after *akṣa*.
*Akṣauhiṇī* means an army. (There is [vṛddhi] after *pra* before *ūha*, *ūḍha*, *ūḍhi*, *eṣa*, and *eṣya*.)
*prauhaḥ*, *prauḍhaḥ*,
*prauḍhiḥ*.

The word *praiṣaḥ* [is derived with the suffix *ghañ*]; likewise *praiṣyaḥ*. [Also, the suffix *ghañ* is applied after the root *iṣ*] when preceded by *ṛte*, except in the case of a compound with a word in the third case (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*).
"Sukhārtaḥ" means "one afflicted by pleasure.
Why [is the word] "third" mentioned?
[To exclude cases such as] "paramārtaḥ" (extremely afflicted).
(Regarding debts for a calf, a heifer, a blanket, clothing, a loan, and a fringe:
*prārṇam*, *vatsatarārṇam*, and so forth.
The *upasargas* [are so called] when they are in conjunction with a verbal action (*kriyā*).

The words beginning with *pra*, when joined with a verbal action, shall be designated as *upasargas* (prepositions). *Pra*, *parā*, *apa*, *sam*, *anu*, *ava*, *nis*, *nir*, *dur*, *dus*, *vi*, *āṅ*, *ni*, *adhi*, *api*, *ati*, *su*, *ut*, *abhi*, *prati*, *para*, and *upa*—these are the *prādayaḥ*.
The roots beginning with *bhū* and *vā* are called *dhātu*.
The verbal roots beginning with *bhū*, which denote action, shall receive the technical designation "dhātu" (verbal root).
When a verbal root begins with the vowel ṛ, the substitution of vṛddhi occurs after a prefix.
When a verbal root beginning with the letter *d* follows an upasarga ending in a vowel other than *a*, the single substitute for both is the *vṛddhi* vowel. For example:
*prārcchati*.
When *eṅ* follows, the single substitute is the form of the subsequent vowel.
When a prefix ending in *ā* is followed by a verbal root beginning with *e* or *o*, a single substitute of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) shall occur. For example:
*prejate*; *upoṣati*.
The suffix *aC* and what follows it is designated as *ṭi*.
Among these vowels, that which is the last is the beginning of that [group]; it shall bear the technical designation *ṭi*.
(In the case of *śakandhu* and similar compounds, a single substitute form is to be stated.
And that [single substitute] takes the place of the *ṭi*.
*śakandhuḥ*,
*karkandhuḥ*, *manīṣā*;
this is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class).
Mārttaṇḍa.
And [the substitution of *ya* occurs] for the case endings *om* and *aṅ*.
When *om* or *āṃ* is followed by *cātpara* (the word *ca* followed by *at*), a single substitute of the form of the subsequent element shall occur.
Examples: *śivāyoṃ namaḥ* and *śiva ehi*.
And [the final and initial sounds] are treated like the end and the beginning.
This single substitute is treated like the final part of the preceding element and like the initial part of the following element; for example: *śivehi*.
When followed by a homogeneous vowel, *a* becomes long.
When a vowel (*ac*) follows, a single long substitute shall take the place of both the preceding and the following sounds when they are homogeneous (*savarṇa*). Examples:
*daityāraḥ* (from *daitya-araḥ*), *śrīśiḥ* (from *śrī-īśiḥ*).
The arising of Viṣṇu; the syllable *hotṛ*.
A long vowel *eṅ* at the end of a word is replaced by *at* when followed by *at*.
When *e* or *o* at the end of a word is followed by *at*, there shall be a single substitute consisting of the preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*). For example: *hare ava*; *viṣṇo ava*.
The word *go* optionally [retains its final vowel length] everywhere.

In both worldly (secular) and Vedic usage, there is optionally the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) for a word ending in *eṅ* before the word *go*, when it occurs at the end of a word. Examples: *goagram* or *go 'gram*.
Why "ending in *eṅ*"? [To exclude cases like *nadyagryam*].
[The suffix] *citragu* [is used] at the end of a word; why [is it not used] at the end of a word? As in *goḥ*.
A substitute consisting of more than one phoneme (anekāl) and beginning with the marker ŚIT replaces the whole of the original element.
This being the position reached:
That which is permanent (ṅit).
But since it consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it would apply only to the final [phoneme].
The substitution of *avaṅ* for *ava* is optional according to Sphoṭāyana.
At the end of a word, the substitute *avaṅ* optionally replaces *go*, which ends in *eṅ*, when followed by *av*. Examples:
*gavāgram* or *go 'gram*. Why "at the end of a word"? Consider: *gavi*.
And [the substitution of *na* for *ṣa* occurs] before *indra*.
When *indra* follows, there should be the substitution of *go-ra*: *gavendraḥ*.
And [the substitution of *e* for *as* occurs] when [a word ending in *as*] is called from a distance.
In addressing someone from a distance, the final syllable (ṭi) of a sentence may optionally be protracted (pluta).
Pluta vowels and pragṛhya vowels are always [unchanged] before a vowel (ac).
These [words] would be natural (*prakṛti*):
"Come, Kṛṣṇa! (three times); "A cow is grazing here."
A dual ending containing *ī*, *ū*, or *e* is *pragṛhya*.
A dual ending that ends in *ī*, *ū*, or *e* is *pragṛhya*. For example:
*harī etau* (these two Hari-s), *viṣṇū imau* (these two Viṣṇu-s), *gaṅge amū* (those two Gaṅgā-s).
The substitute *māt* is applied in place of *adas*.
The dual endings *asmat* and *parau* are *pragṛhya*.
Examples: *amī īśāḥ*;
*rāmakṛṣṇāvamū āsāte*.
"What is it? "In such-and-such a place here."
The group of words beginning with *ca* [are indeclinables] when they do not denote a substance (*asatva*).
Particles such as *ca* and others shall be those whose meaning is not a substance (*adravyārtha*).
The words beginning with *pra* [are called *upasarga* when they are combined with verbal roots].
These also are likewise.
A particle consisting of a single vowel, except for the particle *aṅ*, is called pragṛhya.
A single vowel *e* or *o*, with the exception of the particle *āṅ*, should be treated as a *pragṛhya*. For example:
*i* Indra; *u* Umeśa.
The recollection of the statement is not [the cause];
rather, it is thus: "Do you think so?
Indeed, that is so."
Except when followed by a *ṅit* suffix;
for example, *ā īṣaduṣṇam* becomes *oṣṇam*.
Thus it is said. (VLk 56 = P 1.1.15)
A word ending in *o* that is an indeclinable (*nipāta*) shall be *pragṛhya*. For example: *aho īśāḥ*.
The word "sambuddhau" (in the vocative singular) [is used] for Śākalya, provided it is not a Vedic utterance.

The vowel *o*, when it is a *pragṛhya* (retaining its original form) as a result of being a perfective suffix (*sambuddhi*), remains unchanged before the particle *iti*—provided it is not in a Vedic context.
For example: *viṣṇo iti*, *viṣṇa iti*, or *viṣṇav iti*.
After *maya* and *u*, *vo* optionally replaces *uña*.
The *maya* (the vowels *i*, *ī*, *u*, *ū*, *ṛ*, *ṝ*) is optionally changed to *va* before the particle *uñ* when followed by a vowel.
For example: *kimvuktam* or *kimu uktam*.
According to Śākalya, an *ik* vowel followed by a non-homogeneous vowel becomes short.

The *ik* vowels at the end of a word may optionally become short before a non-homogeneous vowel (*aci*). Because of the force of the rule prescribing this shortening, no vowel sandhi (*svarasandhi*) takes place.
Examples: *cakri atra* or *cakry atra*.
Why specify "at the end of a word"? [Consider: *gaurī-au*.
[This is governed by: *aco rahābhyāṃ dve* (Pāṇini 8.4.46).
A *yar* (any consonant except *h*) following *r* or *h*, which themselves follow a vowel (*ac*), may optionally be doubled. Examples:
*gauryyau* (or *gaurī*). (This does not apply) in a compound: *vāpyaśvaḥ*.
The substitution of *ṛ* for *ṛti* occurs before a suffix marked with the technical term *ak*.
Before the vowel *ṛ*, vowels at the end of a word that are not *a*-sounds (*akaḥ*) optionally undergo the same changes as previously described. For example:
*brahma ṛṣiḥ* becomes *brahmarṣiḥ*.
Why "at the end of a word"? [Consider: *ārchat*.
Thus ends the vowel sandhi; now follows the consonant sandhi:

*stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.40). When the sounds *s*, *t*, or *th* (the *st* group) come into contact with the sounds *ś*, *ṣ*, or *s* (the *śc* group), they are replaced by the sounds *ś*, *ṣ*, or *s* respectively.

When the letter *s* or the *ta*-group (t, th, d, dh, n) is joined with the letter *ś* or the *ca*-group (c, ch, j, jh, ñ), they become *ś* or the *ca*-group respectively. For example: *rāmaśśete* (Rāma lies down);
*rāmaścinoti* (Rāma gathers).
Sacit!
O wielder of the Śārṅga bow, be victorious!
From the root √śā. (Pāṇini 8.4.44)
The substitution of *c* for the following retroflex class (*tavarga*) shall not occur after *ś*. For example:
*viśnaḥ*, *praśnaḥ*.
When a *ṣṭu*-group [consonant] follows, a *ṣṭu*-group [consonant] is substituted [in its place].
When *s* or *t* (the *stoḥ*) are joined with *ṣ*, *ṭ*, or *n* (the *ṣṭunā*), they become *ṣ*, *ṭh*, or *ṇ* (the *ṣṭuḥ*). For example: *rāmaṣṣaṣṭhaḥ*;
*rāmaṣṭīkate*.
The grinder;
the commentary;
you approach the wheel.
The substitution of ṭu for ṣa does not occur when ṣa is at the end of a word, except before the word *anām*.
After a word-final *ṭ*-class consonant, the *s* or *t* of the *st*-group shall not become *ṣ* or *ṭ* when followed by a non-name (*anāman*).
Examples: *ṣaṭ santaḥ*, *ṣaṭ te*.
Why "from the end of a word" (*padāntāt*)? [Consider: *īṭṭe*.
Why "of *ṭ*"? [Consider: *sarpiṣṭamam*. [It should be stated: "Except for *anām*, *navati*, and *nagarī*."
Ninety-six;
six cities.
The substitution of *ṣ* occurs for *t* before *ṣ*.
There is no status as *ṣṭu*. [The word] *san-ṣaṣṭhaḥ* [is an example].
In the final position, the *jaś* sounds replace the *jhal* sounds.
At the end of a word, the *jhal* sounds shall become *jaś* sounds. For example: *vāgīśaḥ*.
A *yara* (the consonants *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*) followed by a nasal (*anunāsika*) may optionally become a nasal.
A final *y* may optionally become nasalized before a following nasal consonant.
Thus: *etanmurāriḥ* or *etad murāriḥ*.
(In the colloquial language, when used as a suffix, it is always [used thus]: *tanmātram* (consisting of that), *cinmayam* (consisting of consciousness).
Before *tor*, [the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*] occurs. // VLk_69 = P_8.4.60 //
When a letter of the *tavarga* (the dental class) is followed by *l*, it is replaced by the corresponding nasal (*parasavarṇa*). For example:
*tallayaḥ*.
The learned one writes:
"In place of *la*, there is an anunāsika [nasal] after *na*.
"After *udaḥ*, [the substitution of] the preceding [vowel occurs] in place of *sthā* and *stambh*. (Pāṇini 8.4.41)
After the word *udak*, the [final] *s* of the roots *sthā* and *stambh* is replaced by a vowel homogeneous with the preceding one.
"Therefore" refers to the subsequent [sūtra].
An operation performed by means of a specification in the fifth case (pañcamī) should be understood as applying to the following [element] that is not separated by another phoneme.
That which is prescribed [by a grammatical rule] applies to that which follows, not to its predecessor.
Whatever is prescribed for a following [sound] should be understood as applying to its initial [consonant].
Thus, *s* becomes *th*.
A *jhar* (a consonant other than *y*, *v*, *r*, or *l*) is dropped before a homogeneous (*savarṇa*) consonant.
A *jhar* sound following a *hal* (consonant) may optionally be elided before a homogeneous (*savarṇa*) *jhar* sound.
And [the substitution of] *khari* [occurs]. (Pāṇini 8.4.55)
By the rule *khari jhalāṃ caraḥ*, the *d* of *ut* becomes *t*; thus,
*utthānam*.
The raising up.
The *jh* sounds [are optionally changed to *gh*] before *ha*, optionally.

"In the impersonal and passive [the ātmanepada endings are used]. (Pāṇini 1.3.13)
The ātmanepada [suffixes] are used after the root *las*.
The suffix *yak* is applied after a verbal root when a *sārvadhātuka* affix follows.
When a *sārvadhātuka* suffix expressing either the action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*) follows a verbal root (*dhātu*), [the suffix is applied].
"Action" (*bhāva*) means activity (*kriyā*); and that is restated by means of a verbal suffix whose meaning is action (*bhāvārthaka*).
Because there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the second or first person pronouns (*yuṣmad* and *asmad*), the third person is used.

Since the action expressed by a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) is not of the nature of a substance (*adravyarūpa*), duality and so forth are not perceived; therefore, the singular number alone is used as the general rule, rather than the dual and so on.
For example: *tvayā mayā anyaiś ca bhūyate* (it is being by you, me, and others), and *babhūve* (it was being).

Before the affixes *syas*, *sīyut*, *tās*, and *iṭ* (the augment *iṭ* added to *liṅ*), when expressing the passive or impersonal voice (*bhāva-karman*), there is optionally the substitution of *ciṇvadbhāva* for roots ending in *a*, *han*, *grah*, or *dṛś*, and the augment *iṭ* is also applied.

According to the *upadeśa*, for those roots ending in *ac* and for *han* and others, there may optionally be an *aṅga*-operation as if it were *ciṇ* when the suffixes beginning with *sya* (the *sya*-class) follow in the sense of the passive (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*). Furthermore, the augment *iṭ* is added to these *sya*-class suffixes.
In the alternative where *ciṇvadbhāva* applies, this *iṭ* is present;
due to *ciṇvadbhāva*, the *vṛddhi* substitution takes place.

it will be caused to come into being.

may it be.

The affix *cleściṇ* shall occur when the verbal suffix *ta*, expressing either the agent (*bhāvaka*) or the object (*karman*), follows; as in *abhāvi* and *abhāviṣyata*.
It would have been so;

[Thus we have] *bhāvitā*, *bhāvayitā*.
It will be brought into being;
it will be cultivated;
it was cultivated.
It may be cultivated;
it may be caused to be cultivated.
He caused [them] to be;
they two caused [them] to be, or they two caused themselves to be.
He desires to exist.
There is lengthening of the vowel before both the *kṛt* and *sārvadhātuka* suffixes.
Viṣṇu is praised (*stūyate*).
[The future forms are] *stāvitā* and *stotā*.
It will be praised; it will be praised. It was praised.
They two were praised; they two were praised.
The root *ṛ* means "to go.

It is that which is sought after (*aryate*).
The root *smṛ* means "to remember.

The augment *iṭ* is applied as if it were *ciṇvadiṭ* due to the inclusion of the term "instruction" (*upadeśa*).
Thus: *āritā*, *artā*;
*smāritā*, *smartā*.
By the rule *aniditām*, there is the elision of the nasal (*n*);
thus, one is "terrified" (*trasyate*).
But when it is marked with the *it* (indicatory letter), as in *nand*, one is "delighted" (*nandyate*).
There is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*); it is sacrificed (*ijyate*).
The substitution of *ya* occurs for the root *tan* when followed by the affix *yak*.
The substitute *ā* may optionally take the place of the final [consonant].
Thus: *tāyate*, *tanyate*.

The affix *ciṇ* shall not occur after the roots *tap*, *śuc*, and *kliś* when used in the sense of the reflexive agent (*karmakartṛ*) or in the sense of repentance (*anutāpa*). For example:
*anvatapta pāpena* ("he was tormented by sin").
[In this case,] by the rule *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām it*, the substitution of *it* for the vowel occurs.
It is given; it is placed; [I] gave.
The suffix *yuk* is added after a verbal root ending in long *ā*, except when the suffixes *ciṇ* or *kṛt* follow.

Thus: *alambhi*, *alābhi*.

Now begins the section on the agentive-passive construction (*karmakartṛprakriyā*):

when the object itself is intended to be expressed as the agent, then, because even transitive verbs become intransitive [in that context], the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) and the impersonal state (*bhāve*).
That which has an action similar to that of an object is treated like an object (karmavat) by virtue of its action.
An agent whose action is equal to the action residing in the object shall be treated like the object;
this is an extension of the grammatical operation (*kāryātideśa*).
By means of this, the passive marker *yaK*, the middle voice endings (*ātmanepada*), and the augment *iṭ* as in *ciṇvadiṭ* shall apply.
The fruit ripens;
the wood is split;

In the sense of "becoming," it is split by means of wood.

Now begins the section on the meaning of the *lakāra*s:
"The suffix *lṛṭ* is used after a verb when there is a statement concerning something already known (*abhijñāvacana*). (Pāṇini 3.2.112)
When *smṛti* or *bodhi* occurs as an upapada, the suffix *lṛṭ* is applied to the verbal root in the sense of the past not belonging to the current day;
this is an exception to *laṅ*.
The root *vas* means "to dwell."
Do you remember, Kṛṣṇa, "We shall dwell in Gokula"? Thus do you perceive and thus do you cognize.

"It was not said during our union, Kṛṣṇa; do you remember what we ate in the forest?"

This is an exception to the *liṭ* [perfect tense].
Yudhiṣṭhira performed sacrifice.
When there is proximity to the present, the verb may optionally be treated as if it were in the present tense.

The suffixes that have been prescribed for the present tense may optionally be used for what is proximate to the present, whether in the past or in the future. For example: *kadā āgato 'si?* ("When did you arrive?
— *ayam āgacchāmi* ("Here I am coming").
This is the traditional teaching:
"When will you go?
"I am going now."
Or I shall go.
The conditional suffix *liṅ* is used to express the cause and that which arises from the cause.
Or it may be: "If one should bow to Kṛṣṇa, one will attain happiness"; "If one will bow to Kṛṣ�ṇa, one will attain happiness" (the future tense is indeed intended here).
Not here;
he flees because [he thinks] "it kills."

The suffix *liṅ* is used for injunction (*vidhi*), invitation (*nimantraṇa*), and so forth. An injunction (*vidhi*) is an instigation, the impelling of an inferior person such as a servant; for example, "One should sacrifice" (*yajeta*).
An invitation (*nimantraṇa*) is the act of assigning a task;
it is the urging of a daughter’s son or others toward a necessary duty such as a *śrāddha* meal, saying,
"One should eat here."
An invitation is permission to act as one wishes;
[it means] "sit here."
*Adhiṣṭa* is an activity preceded by a request; for example:
"May you teach your son."
Inquiry is thorough deliberation: "O sir, shall I study the Veda, or shall I study logic?"
Prārthanā means a request; for example: "O, may I obtain food. Thus is the optative (loṭ).
Thus ends the section on the meaning of the verbal suffixes (lakāra).
Thus ends the section on verbal suffixes (tiṅanta).
Now, regarding the section on primary suffixes (*kṛt*):
the formation of primary suffixes begins from the verbal root (*dhātu*).
From the beginning up to the end of the third chapter, those suffixes (pratyaya) shall follow after a verbal root (dhātu). By the rule *kṛdatiṅ*, they receive the technical designation *kṛt*.
An alternative form [is used] except in the feminine.

In this section concerning gender (*dhatu*), a suffix that is not identical in form (*asarūpa*) to its general rule (*utsarga*) may optionally supersede that general rule, with the exception of those [suffixes] prescribed under the heading of feminine (*stryadhikāra*).
The suffix *kyap* is applied [after verbal roots ending in a vowel] to form feminine nouns denoting an action (*kṛtya*).
The technical designation *kṛtya* applies to [suffixes] prior to the rule beginning with *ṇvultṛcau*.
A *kṛt* suffix occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).

Since it would follow [from the general rule] that "a *kṛt* suffix occurs when the agent (*kartṛ*) is to be expressed," [the sūtra states]: "The *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khal-artha* suffixes occur only with respect to those two [the action and the object]. (Pāṇini 3.4.70)
These [suffixes] occur only in the sense of the agent and the object.
The suffixes *tavyat*, *tavya*, and *anīyar* [are used after a verbal root to form gerundives].
These suffixes are applied after a verbal root:
*edhitavyam* and *edhanīyam* [should be increased] by you.
In the sense of a state (*bhāva*), the default singular number and neuter gender apply. For example:
*dharmas tvayā cetavyo vā cayanīyaḥ* ("the dharma is to be accumulated by you")—here the suffix *kelimar* is added as a supplement;
and *pacelimā māṣāḥ* ("the beans are ready to be cooked").
The meaning is "to be cooked.
*Bhidelimāḥ* means "straight" (or "pliant"); the meaning is "to be split."
The suffix occurs when there is an object of the action.
The suffixes *kṛtya* and *lyuṭ* are used diversely.
In some cases there is application, in some cases non-application, in some cases an option, and in some cases something else entirely;
having observed the various prescriptions of the rule in many ways, they speak of the fourfold *bāhulaka* (the principle of diversity). // 1 //
That by which one bathes is "snānīyam," meaning bathing powder; that to whom something is given is "dānīyaḥ," meaning a Brahmin worthy of a gift.
The suffix *yat* is applied after [a stem ending in] *a*.
The suffix *yat* shall occur after a verbal root ending in a vowel; [the resulting form is] *ceyam*.
The substitution of *ī* occurs before the affix *yat*.
When *pare* follows, *ātaḥ* becomes *īt*:
*deyam*, *gleyam*.
After a verbal root ending in *r* or *l*, [the suffix *yaṅ* is optionally applied].
The suffix *yat* shall be applied after a word ending in a letter of the *pa*-group (*pavarga*) that has *at* as its penultimate vowel; this is an exception to [the application of] *ṇyat*. Examples:
*śapyam*, *labhyam*.
The suffix *kyap* is applied after the verbal roots *i*, *etu*, *śās*, *vṛ*, *dṛ*, and *juṣ*.
The suffix *kyap* shall be applied after these [roots].
The augment *tuk* is added after a short vowel before a *kṛt* suffix that begins with a *p*-sound.
Ityaḥ; stutyaḥ; [the root] śās in the sense of instructing.
The substitution of *śās* for *śāsu* occurs before the affixes *iṭ* and *haL*.
The *upadhā* vowel of the root *śās* is replaced by *it* before an affix beginning with a consonant that has an indicatory *k* or *ṅ*, provided it is not *aṅ*. Thus:
*śiṣyaḥ*;
*vṛtyaḥ*.
To be honored; to be enjoyed.
After the root *mṛj*, [the substitution of *guṇa*] is optional.
The suffix *kyap* is optionally applied after the root *mṛj*; thus, [the form] *mṛjyaḥ*.
The suffix *ṇyat* is added after verbal roots ending in *ṛ* or *hal*.
The suffix *ṇyat* is applied after a verbal root ending in an *ṛ*-vowel or a consonant. Examples:
*kāryam*, *hāryam*, *dhāryam*.
The substitution of *ku* occurs for the sounds *ca* and *ja* before an affix marked with the markers *gh* or *ṇi*.
The substitution of *k* for *c* and *j* occurs when *ghi* or *ṇyat* follows.
In place of the vowel of the root *mṛj*, there is vṛddhi substitution.
The augment *ik* is applied to the root *mṛj*, and there is *vṛddhi* substitution before *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes; [thus] *mārgyaḥ*.
The word *bhojya* is substituted for *bhakṣya*.
The other is the object of enjoyment.
Thus ends the section on the formation of verbal derivatives (*kṛtya-prakriyā*).
Now, [the suffixes] *ṇvul* and *tṛc* [are introduced] after a verbal root that has been previously formed with a *kṛt* suffix.
These two [suffixes] follow a verbal root (dhātu);
by the rule "kṛt suffixes [denote] the agent," they occur when the sense is that of the agent (kartṛ).
In place of the suffixes *yu* and *vu*, the substitutes *an* and *ak* are applied respectively.
In these two cases, the [suffixes] *yu* and *vu* are applied when they do not denote a location (*anākau*).
Examples: *kārakaḥ*, *kartā*.
The suffixes *lyu*, *ṇini*, and *ac* are applied after the words *nandi*, *grahi*, and those beginning with *pac*.
The suffix *lyu* occurs after [roots] such as *nand*,
the suffix *ṇini* after [roots] such as *grah*,
and the suffix *ac* after [roots] such as *pac*.
He delights [the gods], thus he is Nandana;
he crushes people, thus he is Janārdana;
he is Lavaṇa.
Grasping,
abiding,
and contemplating.
The *pacādi* group is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*).
The suffix *ka* is applied after verbal roots ending in *i*, those having *u* or *ū* as their penultimate vowel (*upadha*), and after the roots *jñā*, *prī*, and *kṛ*.
From these, what might [be derived]?
*budhaḥ* (wise),
*kṛśaḥ* (emaciated).
jñaḥ / priyaḥ / kiraḥ //
And [the suffix *ka*] is added after the root *āp* when a prefix (*upasarga*) precedes it.
Wise; easy to overcome.
Who is in the house?
In the sense of "house" (geha), the suffix *ka* should be applied after the root *grah*; thus, *gṛham*.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after a verbal root when it denotes an action related to the agent.
When a word denoting the object (*karman*) is used as an upapada, the suffix *aṇ* shall be added to the verbal root.
For example, "one who makes a jar" (*kumbhaṃ karoti*) is called a *kumbhakāraḥ*.
The suffix *ka* is applied after a verbal root ending in long *ā*, provided it is not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*).

The suffix *ka* shall be applied after a verbal root ending in long *ā*, provided it is not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*), when an object (*karman*) is present as a co-occurring word (*upapada*).
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule for the suffix *aṇ*. [Furthermore,] there is elision (*lopa*) of the final *ā* before a suffix marked with *iṭ* and before *ka*.
A giver of cows, a giver of wealth, a giver of blankets.

*gosandāyaḥ*. (Vārttika: The suffix *ka* is applied after words such as *mūlavibhuja*.

Examples include *mahīdhraḥ* ("earth-bearer") and *kudhraḥ* ("mountain").
The suffix *iṣṭha* is applied after a word denoting a quality (*guṇa*) to express the superlative degree.
When a locus is used as a subordinate word [in composition], [the suffix ṭa is applied]; for example, *kurucaraḥ* ("one who moves in the Kurus").
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after the words *bhikṣā*, *senā*, and *dāya*.
"Begging for alms," "marching with an army," and "having taken"— these are forms ending in the suffix *lyap*.
One who wanders taking [only what is necessary].
The suffix *kvip* is applied after the root *kṛ* when expressing causality, habitual disposition, or conformity.
When these meanings are to be expressed, the suffix *iṣṭhan* shall be applied after the root *kṛ*.
Therefore, [the elision of the case-ending] does not occur after an indeclinable when it precedes *kṛ*, *kami*, *kaṃsa*, *kumbha*, *pātra*, *kuśā*, or *akarṇī*. (Pāṇini 6.3.46)
In a compound, the *visarga* of the final member, provided it is not indeclinable (*avyaya*), is invariably replaced by *s* when followed by words such as *karoti* and others. For example:
*yaśaskarī vidyā* (glory-bestowing knowledge) and *śrāddhakaraḥ* (one who performs the ancestral rites).
One who acts according to what is said.
The suffix *khaś* is applied after the root *ej*.
The suffix *khaś* shall be applied after the root *ej*, when it is followed by the causative marker *ṇi*.
The augment *mum* is added after a word ending in *ar*, *dviṣat*, or a word ending in *ac*, when followed by a word beginning with a vowel.

The augment *mum* is applied after the words *aruṣa*, *dviṣat*, and *ajanta* when followed by the suffix *khid*, but not after an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Because the suffix is marked with *śit*, *śap* and the others are applied.
Thus, one who causes people to tremble is called *janamejaya*.
The suffix *khac* is applied after the root *vad* when preceded by *priya* or *vaśa*.
One who speaks kindly;
one who speaks with authority.
They are also seen after other [roots]. (Pāṇini 3.2.75)
The suffixes *manin*, *kvanip*, *vanip*, and *vic* shall occur after a verbal root.
The suffix *kṛt* does not occur after the root *naś*.
The augment *iṭ* shall not be applied after roots such as *vaś*.
The root *śṝ* is used in the sense of injury.
Suśarman, who comes at dawn.
The nasalized [allophones] of *viṭ*, *van*, and *an* are replaced by *a* when followed by a consonant (*at*).
The substitute *āt* is applied in place of a nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*). Thus, from *vijāyate*, [the word] *vijāvā* is derived.
The root √oṇṛ means "to remove."
avāvā / vic //
The roots *ruṣ* and *riṣ* are used in the sense of harming.
Roṭ / reṭ / sugaṇ.
And the suffix *kvip* [is also applied].
This [suffix] is also seen [in the following examples]:
*ukhāsrat*, *parṇadhvat*, and *bāhabhraṭ*.
The suffix *ṇini* is applied after a verbal root ending in *su* when expressing a genus (*ajāti*), provided it denotes habitual action (*tācchīlya*).

When a *sup*-ending word meaning "non-birth" (i.e., not denoting an action) follows, the suffix *ṇini* is added to a verbal root to express habitual action (*tācchīlya*). Example: *uṣṇabhojī* ("one who habitually eats hot food").
The word *manas* [is used in the sense of the object of the verb *man*]. Pāṇini 3.2.82.
The suffix *ṇini* occurs after the root *man* when it follows a word ending in the accusative case;
for example, *darśanīyamānī*.
And the suffix *khaś* is applied after the verbal root *mān* when it means "to consider oneself."

The suffix *khaś* (which becomes *manya*) is applied after the root *man* when it occurs with an object that is coreferential with the agent, provided a word ending in a *sup* suffix follows; optionally, the suffix *cviṇ* (which becomes *āni*) may also be applied.
One who considers oneself learned is called *paṇḍitamanyaḥ* or *paṇḍitamānī*.
The suffix *khiti* is applied after an indeclinable (*avyaya*).
When the suffix *khid* follows, the first member of the compound takes its short vowel; then *mum* is added. Example: *kālimmanyā*.
The suffix *kyap* is applied after the root *yaj* when it denotes an instrument.

When a word denoting an instrument (karaṇa) is used as an upapada, the suffix *ṇini* is added to the root *yaj* in the sense of the past tense (*bhūta-artha*) to express the agent (*kartṛ*). For example:
*someneṣṭavān* = *somayājī* ("one who has sacrificed with Soma"); *agniṣṭomeneṣṭavān* = *agniṣṭomayājī* ("one who has sacrificed with the Agniṣṭoma").
The suffix *kvanip* is applied after the root *dṛś* (to see).
In the past tense, regarding the object of the action:
one who has seen the further shore is called *pāradṛśvā*.
The suffix *kvip* is applied after the root *kṛ* (to do) when it follows the word *rājan* in the sense of "acting as king" (*yudhi*).

It would be *kvanip*. The root *yudh* has an implied causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*). One who has caused a king to fight is *rājayudhvā*; likewise, one who has caused [something] to be made by a king is *rājakṛtvā*.
And also in the case of *saha*. (Pāṇini 3.2.96)
The word "actions" (*karmaṇi*) is understood [from the previous rule]. *Sahayudhvā* means one who has fought together; *sahakṛtvā* means having acted together.
The suffix *ḍa* is applied after the root *jan* when it occurs in the locative case.
In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the sixth case-affix is diversely applied before a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix.
The elision of *ṅe* [the genitive singular ending] occurs: *sarasijam*, *sarojam*.
And [the suffix *ka* is applied] after a preverb when a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is formed.
*Prajā* occurs in the senses of progeny and people.
The suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu* are called *niṣṭhā*.
These two are designated as "niṣṭhā."
The suffix *niṣṭhā* [is applied after a verbal root].
The *niṣṭhā* suffixes would apply to a verbal root (*dhātu*) that functions in accordance with its actual meaning.
In that context, by the rule "of those two alone," the *kta* suffix occurs in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*);
and by the rule "the *kṛt* suffixes [denote] the agent," the *ktavatu* suffix occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).
The two syllables *uk* have been uttered;
I have bathed;
Viṣṇu has been praised by you.
Viṣṇu has created the universe.
After the two sounds *r* and *d*, the *t* of a *niṣṭhā* suffix is replaced by *n*; and the preceding *d* is also replaced by *n*.
After the two sounds *r* and *d*, the suffix *niṣṭhā* becomes *na*; furthermore, in relation to that *niṣṭhā*, the *d* of the preceding verbal root also becomes *n*.
The root *śṛ* is used in the sense of injury.
After the word *ṛta*,
the letter *n* becomes *ṇ* when followed by a *ra*-paraka vowel.
Decayed; broken; severed.
The suffix *ya* is applied after a verbal root beginning with a vowel that follows a conjunct consonant and ending in *yaṇ*.
The forms *niṣṭhāta*, *drāṇa*, and *glāna* would [be derived] from this [root].
[The suffix *aṇ* is applied] after [the group of words beginning with] *lū*. (Pāṇini 4.1.87)
After the twenty-one roots beginning with *lū*, it is as before:
*lūnaḥ*.
The root *jyā*.
By the rule "grahijyā," there is vocalization (saṃprasāraṇa).
[The suffixes] beginning with *ha* [are termed *ārdhadhātuka*].
When there is a *saṃprasāraṇa* following a consonant after a member of a compound, the vowel at the end of that [member] becomes long. Example: *jīnaḥ*.
And [the suffix *kta*] is applied after a verb that has been stated [to take it].
The root *bhuja* becomes *bhugna*;
from *ṭuośvi*, it becomes *ucchūna*.
